ai.title: Android’s DIY widgets are a bit of vibe-coding fun
ai.brief: You can have a good time brewing up widgets — as long as you don’t expect too much. You can have a good time brewing up widgets — as long as you don’t expect too much. Aside from dealing with my calendar , there’s one thing I want AI to do: tell me if I’m about to miss the bus. What I need is a widget. It needs to tell me real-time arrivals for the bus stop near my house. Tapping around on my phone screen to open the right app and select my stop will slow me down enough to miss a bus. I need glanceable information, and I hoped that Android’s vibe-coded widget feature could help me out here. It hasn’t, to my disappointment, but I still had a good time cooking up other widgets.

sec.title: Unpatched Cacti zero-day with public PoC gives remote code execution
sec.brief: A zero-day vulnerability in the Cacti network monitoring platform has been publicly disclosed, along with a proof-of-concept exploit that lets unauthenticated attackers execute commands on vulnerable servers. The exploit, dubbed " 4HTTP2SHELL " (previously 4HTTP2ROOT), was published on Thanksgiving Day by a cybersecurity researcher known as ek0ms savi0r from the Church of Malware, who demonstrated how the vulnerability can be exploited using just four HTTP requests. Cacti is an open-source network monitoring and graphing tool used to monitor the performance of servers, routers, switches, firewalls, and other network infrastructure. Because the software can store credentials and SNMP passphrases used to access or read data from monitored devices, compromising a Cacti server could potentially give attackers access to other systems on a corporate network. " "I found a path from a fresh, unauthenticated HTTP session to command execution as the Cacti server user in four requests. No login.
